analysis.title: Future of healthcare: Extinction or accelerated evolution?
key_insights: McKinsey says healthcare is in its sixth year of rising costs and falling reimbursement, while AI and biopharma advances open new business models. The author is Shubham Singhal (McKinsey Global Institute).

Payers: 65 to 80 percent of payer jobs are transaction oriented (claims processing) and could be almost fully automated by AI. McKinsey suggests AI agents reviewing electronic medical records could make claims unnecessary, with payers becoming data and intelligence platforms, compared to stock exchanges selling indexes and data products.

Another 10 to 25 percent of payer jobs are knowledge oriented (actuaries, medical management nurses). McKinsey estimates up to 50 percent efficiency gains, which could fund risk-aligned payment models such as carving cancer risk out of employer plans and sharing it across payer, oncologist, health system and pharma.

Primary care: AI-enhanced direct primary care (DPC, a membership-fee model) could raise physician panels from about 400 to more than 3,000 patients. DPC physicians are not paid per visit, so productivity gains are not a revenue loss.

H.R. 1 now lets the more than 59 million Americans with health savings accounts use pre-tax dollars for DPC fees. Utah's 2026 Doctronic pilot had AI autonomously renew 192 chronic medications with a 99.2 percent match to physician decisions.

Acute care: the healthcare productivity growth gap versus the US economy was about three percentage points from 2019 to 2025. McKinsey cites pressure from Medicare volume growth, reimbursement cuts, site neutral payment and Medicare for All proposals, and says profitability at Medicare rates is imperative.

Hospitals should prioritize ambulatory sites with higher growth and ROIC and raise utilization of existing assets rather than build capacity. McKinsey estimates an operating room used like an airline uses aircraft would see 2.5 times its current weekly utilization. It also expects acute procedure demand may fall in many regions over 30 years due to demographics and GLP-1 drugs.

Biopharma access: consumer-direct models for GLP-1 drugs are growing. The share of Zepbound prescriptions initiated through LillyDirect rose from 25 percent in Q1 2025 to 55 percent in Q2 2026, and Eli Lilly expanded self-pay pricing to major pharmacies in March 2026.

High-cost treatments such as cell and gene therapies could use outcomes-based, spread-out payments, center of excellence delivery with shared risk, and employer plan carve-outs. McKinsey also floats reinsurance or securities contracts that hedge treatment costs against pharma revenues or equity values.

Healthcare services and technology (HST) has been the fastest growing and most resilient profit pool. McKinsey says the moat comes from deep integration in clinician workflows and from platforms other solutions depend on. It names revenue cycle management as a services-centric workflow ripe for AI disruption and says measurable cost or efficiency benefit is table stakes.
McKinsey expects healthcare employment to grow rather than shrink despite AI job-loss concerns, because demand is rising and access is inadequate. The industry employs more than 20 million people.

Execution constraint: AI improves exponentially, core technology modernization is linear, and organizational change is slower still. McKinsey recommends a semantic layer that decouples new products from legacy core systems, and warns that a majority of change efforts fail.

sector_views.rationale: Claims processing work faces near-full automation, but McKinsey sees payers surviving as data platforms if they move to value-added products.
Described as the fastest growing and most resilient profit pool, with AI-integrated, workflow-embedded businesses best positioned.
Reimbursement pressure, site neutral payment risk, a productivity gap and possible long-run demand decline, with ambulatory sites the better place for capital.
AI could multiply physician panel sizes and HSA eligibility removes a payment barrier.

earnings_insights: Eli Lilly earnings calls (Q1 2025 and Q2 2026), as cited by McKinsey: the share of Zepbound prescriptions initiated through LillyDirect rose from 25 percent in Q1 2025 to 55 percent in Q2 2026. These are company-reported figures, not estimates.
Eli Lilly announced in March 2026 that it was expanding self-pay pricing on the new Zepbound beyond LillyDirect to major pharmacies nationwide.
risk_factors: Organizational change is slow, a majority of change efforts fail to reach their objectives, and organizations show recidivism in their change efforts.
Legacy core technology modernizes only linearly, which limits how fast AI value can be captured.
Possible disintermediation of incumbents by industry-adjacent participants or new entrants.
Further regulatory and reimbursement pressure, including site neutral payment and Medicare for All proposals.
Many of the payer risk-sharing models would require regulatory changes.
Autonomous AI in clinical settings requires clinical safeguards, and patient consent, privacy and data governance for any engagement platform.
A long-run decline in acute procedure demand from demographics and GLP-1 therapies could strand hospital capital with a 30 to 40 year cycle.
geopolitical: Legislative proposals like Medicare for All and site neutral payment are cited as threats to hospital reimbursement.
H.R. 1 (the One Big Beautiful Bill) guidance from Treasury and the IRS on December 9, 2025 lets HSA holders use pre-tax dollars for direct primary care fees.
McKinsey warns a further decline in public trust in healthcare could intensify calls for major government action.

key_data_points.metric: Share of physicians using OpenEvidence daily
key_data_points.context: Cited from McKinsey Consumer Health Insights Survey 2026 and OpenEvidence's January 2026 release as evidence of rapid AI adoption.
key_data_points.anchor: more than 40 percent of physicians using OpenEvidence daily

key_data_points.metric: Private capital available to deploy into healthcare
key_data_points.context: Assumes healthcare captures 15 to 20 percent of $2.2 trillion in available private capital.
key_data_points.anchor: an estimated $330 billion to $440 billion available to deploy

key_data_points.metric: Share of payer jobs that are transaction oriented
key_data_points.context: McKinsey says AI could fully automate all or almost all of these jobs.
key_data_points.anchor: At a typical payer, 65 to 80 percent of jobs are transaction oriented

key_data_points.metric: AI efficiency gain for payer knowledge-oriented jobs
key_data_points.context: McKinsey estimate. Knowledge-oriented jobs are 10 to 25 percent of payer jobs.
key_data_points.anchor: AI could deliver, in our estimation, as much as 50 percent greater efficiency in these jobs

key_data_points.metric: Potential panel size for an AI-augmented direct primary care physician
key_data_points.context: Compared with a current average of about 400 patients per DPC physician.
key_data_points.anchor: could potentially serve more than 3,000 patients, according to our research

key_data_points.metric: Match rate of AI prescription renewals to physician decisions in Utah's 2026 Doctronic pilot
key_data_points.context: AI renewed 192 commonly prescribed chronic medications. Physicians reviewed the first 250 patients before action and the next 1,000 retroactively.
key_data_points.anchor: had a 99.2 percent match rate to physician decisions

key_data_points.metric: Americans covered by health savings accounts who can now use pre-tax dollars for DPC fees
key_data_points.context: Enabled by H.R. 1, with IRS guidance dated December 9, 2025.
key_data_points.anchor: the more than 59 million Americans covered by health savings accounts (HSAs)

key_data_points.metric: Productivity growth gap between healthcare delivery and the overall US economy, 2019 to 2025
key_data_points.context: Based on BLS and BEA data. McKinsey says closing it would double the standard of living from one generation to the next.
key_data_points.anchor: The productivity growth gap between healthcare delivery and the overall US economy from 2019 to 2025 was about three percentage points

key_data_points.metric: Estimated operating room weekly utilization if used like airlines use aircraft
key_data_points.context: McKinsey estimate used to illustrate asset utilization upside for hospitals.
key_data_points.anchor: we estimate that it would see 2.5 times its current weekly utilization

key_data_points.metric: Share of Zepbound prescriptions initiated through LillyDirect, Q1 2025 to Q2 2026
key_data_points.context: Taken from Eli Lilly earnings calls for Q1 2025 and Q2 2026.
key_data_points.anchor: the share of Zepbound prescriptions initiated through LillyDirect jumped from 25 percent in the first quarter of 2025 to 55 percent in the second

key_data_points.metric: Reduction in molecule discovery time from AI in drug development
key_data_points.context: Based on McKinsey experience. Also cites 1.5 times new molecular entities for the same costs and a 10 to 30 percent better probability of success in clinical development.
key_data_points.anchor: By a 70 to 80 percent reduction in molecule discovery time, 1.5 times new molecular entities launched for the same costs

key_data_points.metric: Length of the hospital capital cycle
key_data_points.anchor: the hospital capital cycle is 30 to 40 years long, in our experience

key_data_points.metric: Increase in average American health span this century
key_data_points.context: Compared with a two-year increase in lifespan. Based on IHME's Global Burden of Disease 2021 study.
key_data_points.anchor: their health span (years lived in good health) has increased by only eight months

tension_points.bull_case: Demand for healthcare services is rising and access is inadequate, so McKinsey expects healthcare employment to grow rather than contract even as AI automates payer transaction work.
tension_points.bear_case: Concerns about AI-driven job loss abound, and the report says AI could fully automate 65 to 80 percent of typical payer jobs and lift knowledge-worker efficiency by up to 50 percent.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI lets DPC physicians serve far more patients without losing revenue because they are paid by membership rather than per visit.
theme_stances.evidence: continuous access to high-quality primary care to all individuals on demand

theme_stances.key_argument: AI could automate most transaction-oriented payer work and turn payers into data platforms.
theme_stances.evidence: AI could fully automate all or almost all of these jobs

theme_stances.key_argument: Capital should go to ambulatory sites with higher growth and ROIC and to raising utilization of existing assets rather than new capacity.
